findings.text: Congo's cobalt exports are now limited by government quotas through 2027, so supply is tight whatever we decide on ethics. Any new rule that cuts out suppliers shrinks an already small pool, and that is a real continuity risk.

We buy battery packs, not cobalt, so the cheapest and fastest checks go through our existing battery suppliers by asking them to name their refiners. Paying for our own audits at a mine we do not buy from directly is a much bigger and slower job.

Right now we cannot link our batteries to TFM or any refiner, and the mine's ownership records disagree. That makes it hard to justify spending a lot on this one mine before we know it is actually in our chain.

challenges.text: A paid labour check at TFM and along the trading route makes sense only if TFM is in our chain, and no evidence shows that yet. Map our own refiners first, then audit the sites that actually show up.

Requiring water, tailings and emissions monitoring for both mine and refiner before any new contract could freeze buying while quotas already squeeze supply. Phasing it in by renewal date gets the data without a supply gap.

feasibility.recommendation: Suppliers name their cobalt refiners in writing with chain-of-custody evidence
feasibility.note: Assumption: a supplier questionnaire and contract clause add small admin cost, though full chain-of-custody records may take suppliers months to gather.

feasibility.recommendation: Refiners must pass an independent responsible-sourcing audit based on ILO rules
feasibility.note: Assumption: accept existing third-party refiner audits first, which limits cost, and set a deadline for those without one.

feasibility.recommendation: Fund an independent labour check at TFM and on the trading route, with worker interviews and a reporting channel
feasibility.note: Assumption: this is costly and slow, and is worth it once refiner mapping shows TFM cobalt is in our batteries (M2).

feasibility.recommendation: Fix problems with suppliers and support affected children instead of dropping suppliers
feasibility.note: Assumption: this also protects continuity, since dropping suppliers in a quota-limited market (D3) is risky; the cost depends on what is found.

feasibility.recommendation: Independent water, tailings and emissions data from mine and refiner before any new contract
feasibility.note: Assumption: making it a hard condition right away could delay contracts by weeks or months, so tie it to renewals.

feasibility.recommendation: Keep a risk register labelling each item as documented, indicator, inference or missing
feasibility.note: Assumption: internal work with small cost that cuts the risk of making claims we cannot back up.

feasibility.recommendation: Factor DRC export quotas into sourcing plans, and put substitute supply through the same checks
feasibility.note: Assumption: checking new suppliers adds weeks to onboarding, but it stops a rushed switch to unknown refiners (D3, M1).

priority_views.cost: Do the cheap moves now: refiner disclosure clauses, the risk register and accepting existing refiner audits. Hold off on paying for our own site audits until we know which mines are really in our chain.
priority_views.speed: Keep buying from current suppliers and add the new requirements at contract renewals, not as conditions that hold up deliveries now. With export quotas in place (D3), we cannot afford a supply gap while suppliers collect paperwork.
priority_views.responsible: Require named refiners, chain-of-custody records and independent audits on a set timeline, and use the results to target site audits and fixes. That costs more and takes longer, but it is the only way to show our cobalt is kept apart from risky hand-dug mines (I3, K3).
